it.title: Il mercato dei dati di addestramento AI con Gabe Greenberg
it.summary: In questo episodio di Latent Space, il fondatore di G2i Gabe Greenberg analizza con swyx le dinamiche economiche dietro l'acquisizione dei dati per i modelli di intelligenza artificiale, discutendo di esclusività e strategie d'ordine.
it.why_it_matters: Comprendere come i laboratori di frontiera scelgono e pagano i dati di addestramento offre uno sguardo privilegiato sulle leve economiche che guidano lo sviluppo dei sistemi di intelligenza artificiale.
it.extended_analysis:
Il mercato dei dati di addestramento rappresenta un pilastro fondamentale e spesso poco visibile nell'evoluzione dei modelli di frontiera. Durante l'intervista condotta da swyx, Gabe Greenberg di G2i spiega le scelte strategiche che spingono un laboratorio a pagare di più per l'esclusività dei dati o ad accettare sconti per dataset condivisi con altri.

L'analisi approfondisce anche la transizione commerciale, mostrando come i piccoli ordini pilota si trasformino in contratti di fornitura più consistenti. Per chi osserva il settore, comprendere questi meccanismi economici aiuta a decifrare le risorse necessarie per alimentare la ricerca avanzata.
it.context: Nel panorama attuale dell'intelligenza artificiale, la disponibilità e la qualità dei dati di addestramento sono fattori critici per il progresso dei modelli, influenzando direttamente i costi e le performance dei laboratori di ricerca.
key_takeaways: I laboratori di frontiera valutano l'esclusività dei dati in base a costi e strategie competitive.
È possibile ottenere sconti sui dati di addestramento se altre aziende possono acquistarli.
I piccoli ordini pilota costituiscono spesso il punto di partenza per transazioni commerciali più ampie.
highlights: Gabe Greenberg di G2i è ospite del podcast Latent Space condotto da swyx.
Vengono discusse le decisioni economiche che regolano il mercato dei dati di addestramento.

en.title: Inside the AI Training Data Market with Gabe Greenberg
en.summary: On Latent Space, G2i founder Gabe Greenberg joins swyx to break down how frontier labs make financial decisions regarding exclusive training data versus shared datasets and pilot orders.
en.why_it_matters: Examining how AI labs acquire training data sheds light on the commercial strategies and economic pressures shaping the development of frontier models.
en.extended_analysis:
The market for AI training data is a critical component of modern machine learning development, yet much of its inner workings remain opaque. In this episode, G2i founder Gabe Greenberg shares insights with host swyx on how frontier labs weigh the costs of exclusive data access against discounted options available to competitors.

The conversation also explores the business pipeline, detailing how initial pilot orders scale into larger commercial agreements. Understanding these dynamics offers a clearer picture of the financial resources and market structures driving the current generation of AI technologies.
en.context: As AI models scale in size and complexity, securing high-quality training data has become a primary operational challenge and a major investment area for research laboratories.
key_takeaways: Frontier labs decide between paying a premium for exclusive data or taking discounts on shared sets.
Small pilot orders often serve as the entry point for larger data procurement deals.
Market dynamics dictate how data providers negotiate with major AI laboratories.
highlights: Gabe Greenberg, founder of G2i, discusses the AI training data market with host swyx.
The episode highlights decision-making frameworks behind lab data acquisition.

es.title: El mercado de datos de entrenamiento en IA con Gabe Greenberg
es.summary: En este episodio de Latent Space, el fundador de G2i, Gabe Greenberg, conversa con swyx sobre cómo los laboratorios de vanguardia deciden entre adquirir datos exclusivos o aceptar descuentos en datos compartidos.
es.why_it_matters: Analizar la adquisición de datos de entrenamiento permite comprender mejor las presiones económicas y las estrategias comerciales detrás del desarrollo de modelos avanzados.
es.extended_analysis:
El mercado de datos para la inteligencia artificial es un factor determinante en la evolución tecnológica actual. Durante la charla, Gabe Greenberg detalla a swyx los criterios económicos que emplean los laboratorios al evaluar la exclusividad de los datos frente a opciones compartidas.

Además, la conversación aborda la evolución comercial, explicando la transición desde pedidos piloto iniciales hasta acuerdos de mayor envergadura. Estos detalles ofrecen una perspectiva valiosa sobre el funcionamiento interno de la industria.
es.context: La obtención de datos de entrenamiento de alta calidad representa uno de los mayores desafíos financieros y operativos para los laboratorios que desarrollan sistemas de inteligencia artificial.
key_takeaways: Los laboratorios evalúan pagar más por la exclusividad de los datos o aceptar descuentos si otros pueden comprarlos.
Los pedidos piloto pequeños suelen escalar hacia contratos de mayor volumen.
La discusión detalla las decisiones estratégicas en el mercado de datos para IA.
highlights: Gabe Greenberg de G2i es entrevistado por swyx en el podcast Latent Space.
Se analizan las decisiones de compra y exclusividad de datos en laboratorios de IA.

de.title: Einblicke in den Markt für KI-Trainingsdaten mit Gabe Greenberg
de.summary: In dieser Episode von Latent Space spricht G2i-Gründer Gabe Greenberg mit swyx darüber, wie Spitzenlabore finanzielle Entscheidungen zwischen exklusiven Trainingsdaten und geteilten Datensätzen treffen.
de.why_it_matters: Die Untersuchung, wie KI-Labore Trainingsdaten beschaffen, verdeutlicht die wirtschaftlichen Strategien und den Druck, die die Entwicklung von Frontmodellen prägen.
de.extended_analysis:
Der Markt für KI-Trainingsdaten ist ein entscheidender, aber oft undurchsichtiger Faktor bei der Entwicklung moderner Modelle. Im Gespräch mit Moderator swyx erläutert Gabe Greenberg die wirtschaftlichen Überlegungen, die Labore bei der Entscheidung zwischen exklusiven Daten und rabattierten, geteilten Datensätzen anstellen.

Zudem wird beleuchtet, wie sich kleine Pilotaufträge zu größeren kommerziellen Vereinbarungen entwickeln. Diese Einblicke helfen dabei, die finanziellen Strukturen hinter der Erforschung und Entwicklung fortschrittlicher Systeme besser zu verstehen.
de.context: Die Sicherung hochwertiger Trainingsdaten stellt eine zentrale operative Herausforderung und einen bedeutenden Investitionsbereich für Forschungslabore dar, die künstliche Intelligenz entwickeln.
key_takeaways: Spitzenlabore wägen zwischen Aufpreisen für exklusive Daten und Rabatten bei geteilten Datensätzen ab.
Kleine Pilotaufträge dienen häufig als Einstieg für größere Beschaffungsverträge.
Das Gespräch beleuchtet die wirtschaftlichen Abläufe auf dem Markt für KI-Daten.
highlights: Gabe Greenberg von G2i ist zu Gast im Podcast Latent Space mit swyx.

items.title: Context Scaling: A New Frontier of AI Scaling
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33160v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many failures of deployed AI arise not from weak inference but from a mismatch between the state a task depends on and the context available when the system acts. Relevant user state, repository revisions, tool traces, sensor readings, or environment changes may be unavailable, distorted, or poorly selected. We call the effort to reduce this bottleneck context scaling. We frame a model as $P_\theta(d\mid c)$ within a system governed by three budgets: training $B_\theta$, decision-time $B_d$, and context-infrastructure $B_c$. Pretraining scaling invests in $\theta$; decision-time scaling searches, refines, or verifies decisions under supplied context; context scaling improves the system's capacity to acquire, represent, deliver, evaluate, and persist deployment state for model use. The three programs interact, but only $B_c$ targets what the system can make available before a decision. This view makes the model-infrastructure pair the unit of analysis. We define effective-context value as a task- and intervention-dependent attribution, separate deployment state from model-visible context, and identify availability, fidelity, selection, and utilization failures. We then organize current mechanisms through a five-operation context lifecycle and propose controlled budget interventions and utility-cost curves for evaluation. The resulting agenda centers on grounded reporting, interaction-data and full-cost infrastructure, and safety and governance for persistent, adaptive systems.

items.title: Constraint-Aware Test-Time Scoring for LLM and VLM Candidate Selection
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When an LLM or VLM produces several candidate answers, picking the best one usually relies on the model's own confidence, a learned judge model, or a domain check. Each has a known weakness: an answer can be fluent but insecure, mathematically plausible but physically infeasible, or rated highly by a judge while quietly breaking a task requirement. We propose a scoring framework that combines a small set of hard checks every answer must pass with a wider set of softer checks whose scores are blended into one number per candidate. This adaptive scoring framework consists of three components: a drafting model that produces the candidates, a configuring model that selects and weights the checks for each task, and scoring models that rate properties no grounded tool can compute. We apply our proposed method to four tasks: writing code that is both correct and secure (CWEval), generating robot manipulation plans (LIBERO with added safety variants), passing competitive-programming hidden tests (LiveCodeBench), and answering questions from retrieved documents (HotpotQA). An ablation study isolates the contribution of each component and finds that the largest gains come from combining hard checks with candidate comparison: on tasks where the first sampled answer is often broken or unsafe, this pairing lifts joint correctness-and-safety by up to +0.21 (retrieval-augmented QA) and code-generation safety by up to +0.28 (CWEval), with the size of the gain tracking how weak the first sample is, falling to near zero or slightly negative where it is already strong. items.title: AutoformBench: A Lean Formalization Benchmark for Advanced Mathematics
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33165v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI systems are increasingly capable of producing machine-checked Lean proofs of advanced mathematical results. Real mathematical formalization, however, is not isolated theorem proving: it requires building the definitions and intermediate lemmas that connect a result to a formal library. Existing evaluations often provide isolated theorem statements in settings where much of this supporting theory is already available in Mathlib. We introduce AutoformBench, a benchmark of 341 Lean 4 formalization tasks drawn from 24 advanced mathematical sources. Lean-experienced mathematicians formalized and audited each target statement, leaving the corresponding Lean proof to the evaluated agent. Each problem is embedded in a broader mathematical development: agents receive the informal proof but must translate it into Lean while constructing the missing definitions, intermediate lemmas, and supporting infrastructure. We compare the performance of frontier models on these problems. We find a largely shared difficulty frontier: success depends less on mathematical domain than on models' ability to construct missing formal infrastructure. Data and code at https://github.com/facebookresearch/autoformbench

items.title: General-Purpose Decision Models for AI Configuration Tuning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33190v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI configuration tuning searches for settings that improve the performance of AI systems under a limited budget. Existing tuners use different sampling and search policies, making the choice of decision strategy central to both tuning quality and cost. We investigate whether general-purpose decision models can guide tuning, using Jev as a deployed representative that returns structured choices and numeric scores across diverse tasks. To assess where it helps, we compare its use as an optimizer, performance predictor, and region guider against conventional methods and a large language model (LLM) on eight AI tuning tasks. Conventional optimizers attain rank 1 in six of eight comparisons. Similarly, established predictors outperform Jev in seven. Through region guidance, however, it finds configurations with lower perplexity than those selected by the native tuner, offering a quality gain when additional decision time and API fees are acceptable. These findings yield actionable recommendations on selecting the decision role, retaining conventional predictors, and balancing tuning quality against cost.

items.title: What, Who, and When: Structured Harm Assessment for Mental Health Safety via Short Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33263v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing use of large language models (LLMs) for mental health support raises important safety concerns. Existing guard models primarily identify categories of harmful content, often overlooking the context needed to determine an appropriate response. We introduce a clinically grounded taxonomy that characterizes harm along three dimensions: what the harm is, who is involved, and when it occurs. It further separates harm characterization from intervention decisions, thus enabling safety policies to be specified outside the model weights through explicit, clinician-curated instructions that can be updated and audited. We validate the taxonomy with expert clinicians and validate a panel of LLM judges to scale annotation. Relabeling public benchmarks in this taxonomy shows that they rarely contain harm directed at the user, which accounts for nearly half of the harm in real conversations. We then train MindGuard2, a 35B-A3B reasoning-based guard model using supervised fine-tuning on short reasoning traces followed by reinforcement learning with a reasoning-length penalty, to minimize inference overhead while preserving the benefits of reasoning. On two public benchmarks and real-world conversations, MindGuard2 achieves balanced accuracy comparable to the substantially larger GLM-5.3 at approximately 10x lower median latency, advancing the accuracy-latency Pareto frontier. Furthermore, it achieves low false-positive rates at high recall, helping balance the need to detect unsafe situations against the risk of unnecessary interventions that may disrupt support and undermine user trust. it.title: MindGuard2: sicurezza nella salute mentale con modelli di linguaggio
it.summary: Ricercatori presentano una tassonomia clinica per la sicurezza nella salute mentale dei modelli linguistici, separando la caratterizzazione del danno dalle decisioni di intervento. Questo approccio ha permesso di sviluppare MindGuard2, un modello di guardia da 35B-A3B addestrato con ragionamento breve e apprendimento rinforzato.
it.why_it_matters: Il modello raggiunge un'accuratezza paragonabile a sistemi molto più grandi come GLM-5.3 ma con una latenza inferiore di circa 10 volte, migliorando il rapporto tra precisione ed efficienza nei contesti di supporto psicologico.
it.extended_analysis:
L'uso crescente dei modelli linguistici nel supporto alla salute mentale solleva serie questioni di sicurezza, poiché i sistemi di controllo tradizionali spesso identificano le categorie di contenuto dannoso senza considerare il contesto cruciale per una risposta adeguata. La nuova tassonomia sviluppata si articola su tre dimensioni: cosa accade, chi è coinvolto e quando si verifica. Separare la caratterizzazione del danno dalle decisioni di intervento consente di specificare le politiche di sicurezza tramite istruzioni curate da clinici e aggiornabili separatamente dai pesi del modello.

Per scalare l'annotazione, il team ha validato un pannello di giudici basati su LLM e addestrato MindGuard2 utilizzando un fine-tuning supervisionato su tracce di ragionamento brevi, seguito da un apprendimento rinforzato con penalità sulla lunghezza del ragionamento. Tale configurazione riduce al minimo l'overhead di calcolo preservando i vantaggi del ragionamento analitico.

Nei test su benchmark pubblici e conversazioni reali, MindGuard2 ottiene tassi di falsi positivi bassi a fronte di un elevato richiamo, bilanciando il rilevamento del pericolo con la riduzione di interventi superflui che potrebbero compromettere la fiducia dell'utente. Vengono rilasciati il modello di guardia con prestazioni di livello superiore, dati sintetici e relative annotazioni.
it.context: I modelli di linguaggio di grandi dimensioni (LLM) sono sempre più impiegati in contesti di supporto alla salute mentale, rendendo essenziale lo sviluppo di barriere di sicurezza affidabili e trasparenti che non introducano eccessivi ritardi operativi.
key_takeaways: Tassonomia clinica tridimensionale: cosa, chi e quando.
MindGuard2 (35B-A3B) riduce la latenza di circa 10 volte rispetto a GLM-5.3.
Bassi tassi di falsi positivi con elevato richiamo per preservare la fiducia dell'utente.
highlights: Separazione tra caratterizzazione del danno e decisioni di intervento.
Addestramento tramite fine-tuning supervisionato e apprendimento rinforzato con penalità sulla lunghezza.

en.title: MindGuard2: Structured Harm Assessment for Mental Health Safety in LLMs
en.summary: Researchers introduce a clinically grounded taxonomy for mental health safety in language models, separating harm characterization from intervention decisions. This approach enables the training of MindGuard2, a 35B-A3B reasoning-based guard model offering low inference latency.
en.why_it_matters: MindGuard2 achieves balanced accuracy comparable to the much larger GLM-5.3 at roughly 10x lower median latency, advancing the accuracy-latency frontier for sensitive mental health applications.
en.extended_analysis:
The growing adoption of large language models for mental health support brings critical safety concerns, as existing guard models frequently overlook the context required to determine correct responses. The proposed taxonomy characterizes harm along three dimensions: what the harm is, who is involved, and when it occurs. By separating harm characterization from intervention decisions, safety policies can be explicitly defined through clinician-curated instructions outside the model weights.

To scale annotation, the authors validated a panel of LLM judges and trained MindGuard2 using supervised fine-tuning on short reasoning traces followed by reinforcement learning with a reasoning-length penalty. This minimizes inference overhead while retaining analytical benefits.

Evaluated on public benchmarks and real-world conversations, MindGuard2 exhibits low false-positive rates at high recall, helping prevent unnecessary interventions that might disrupt user trust. The team has released the guardrail model along with synthetic conversations and annotations.
en.context: As language models see broader adoption in mental health applications, robust guardrails are essential to detect risks accurately without introducing prohibitive computational overhead or disrupting user support.
key_takeaways: Clinically grounded taxonomy characterizing harm by what, who, and when.
MindGuard2 achieves performance comparable to GLM-5.3 with ~10x lower latency.
Low false-positive rate combined with high recall to protect user trust.
highlights: Decoupling harm characterization from intervention rules via clinician-curated instructions.
Training via supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with a reasoning-length penalty.

es.title: MindGuard2: Evaluación estructurada de daños para la salud mental en LLM
es.summary: Investigadores presentan una taxonomía clínica para la seguridad en salud mental de los modelos de lenguaje, separando la caracterización del daño de las decisiones de intervención. Esto permite entrenar a MindGuard2, un modelo de guardia basado en razonamiento de 35B-A3B.
es.why_it_matters: MindGuard2 alcanza una precisión equilibrada comparable a la del mucho mayor GLM-5.3 con una latencia media aproximadamente 10 veces menor, mejorando la eficiencia en aplicaciones de salud mental.
es.extended_analysis:
El uso creciente de grandes modelos de lenguaje (LLM) para el apoyo en salud mental plantea importantes retos de seguridad, ya que los modelos de control existentes suelen omitir el contexto necesario para una respuesta adecuada. La taxonomía introducida caracteriza el daño en tres dimensiones: qué es, quién está implicado y cuándo ocurre. Al separar la caracterización del daño de las decisiones de intervención, las políticas de seguridad pueden especificarse mediante instrucciones curadas por clínicos fuera de los pesos del modelo.

Para escalar la anotación, se validó un panel de jueces LLM y se entrenó MindGuard2 mediante ajustes finos supervisados con trazas de razonamiento corto, seguidos de aprendizaje reforzado con penalización por longitud de razonamiento. Esto reduce la sobrecarga de inferencia manteniendo los beneficios analíticos.

En evaluaciones con benchmarks públicos y conversaciones reales, MindGuard2 logra bajas tasas de falsos positivos con alta recuperación, ayudando a equilibrar la detección de riesgos y evitando interrupciones innecesarias en el soporte al usuario.
es.context: La expansión de los modelos de lenguaje en el ámbito de la salud mental exige mecanismos de seguridad rigurosos que operen de forma eficiente y eviten falsas alarmas que erosionen la confianza del usuario.
key_takeaways: Taxonomía clínica tridimensional: qué, quién y cuándo.
MindGuard2 ofrece precisión similar a GLM-5.3 con una latencia 10 veces inferior.
Baja tasa de falsos positivos y alta recuperación para proteger la confianza del usuario.
highlights: Separación de la caracterización del daño y las reglas de intervención.
Entrenamiento con ajuste fino supervisado y aprendizaje reforzado.

zh-CN.title: MindGuard2：基于短推理的心理健康安全结构化危害评估
zh-CN.summary: 研究人员为大语言模型的心理健康安全引入了一套基于临床基础的分类法，将危害表征与干预决策相分离。该方法催生了MindGuard2，一个采用短推理轨迹训练的35B-A3B推理型护栏模型。
zh-CN.why_it_matters: MindGuard2实现了与体积大得多的GLM-5.3相当的平衡准确率，而中位延迟降低了约10倍，树立了兼顾准确性与低延迟的新标准。
zh-CN.extended_analysis:
大语言模型在心理健康支持中的应用日益广泛，这引发了重要的安全隐患，因为现有的防护模型往往忽略了确定适当回应所需的上下文。研究中提出的分类法从三个维度表征危害：危害是什么、涉及谁以及何时发生。通过将危害表征与干预决策分开，安全策略可以通过外部的、经临床医生审定的指令进行指定，从而独立于模型权重进行更新。

为了扩大注释规模，团队验证了一组LLM评判员，并使用短推理轨迹的监督微调以及带有推理长度惩罚的强化学习来训练MindGuard2，从而在保留推理优势的同时将推理开销降至最低。

在公开基准测试和真实对话的评估中，MindGuard2在保持高召回率的同时实现了较低的误报率，有助于在检测不安全情况与避免可能破坏用户信任的不必要干预之间取得平衡。团队同时发布了该防护模型及合成数据。
zh-CN.context: 随着语言模型更广泛地应用于心理健康领域，开发能够准确检测风险且不会带来过高计算延迟的强大安全护栏变得至关重要。
key_takeaways: 基于临床的三维度分类法：危害是什么、涉及谁以及何时发生。
MindGuard2的性能与GLM-5.3相当，但延迟降低约10倍。
在维持高召回率的同时实现低误报率，保护用户信任。
highlights: 将危害表征与干预决策解耦，采用临床医生审定的指令进行管理。
通过监督微调和带有长度惩罚的强化学习进行训练。

de.title: MindGuard2: Strukturierte Schadensbewertung für psychische Sicherheit in LLMs
de.summary: Forschende stellen eine klinisch fundierte Taxonomie für die psychische Sicherheit von Sprachmodellen vor, die Schadenscharakterisierung und Interventionsentscheidungen trennt. Dies ermöglicht die Entwicklung von MindGuard2, einem 35B-A3B-Schutzmodell auf Basis kurzer Argumentationsschritte.
de.why_it_matters: MindGuard2 erreicht eine vergleichbare Genauigkeit wie das deutlich größere GLM-5.3 bei einer um das Zehnfache geringeren medianen Latenz, womit die Effizienzgrenze für sensible Anwendungen verschoben wird.
de.extended_analysis:
Der zunehmende Einsatz großer Sprachmodelle in der psychischen Unterstützung wirft wichtige Sicherheitsfragen auf, da bestehende Schutzmodelle oft den Kontext übersehen, der für eine angemessene Reaktion erforderlich ist. Die eingeführte Taxonomie charakterisiert Schaden anhand von drei Dimensionen: Was der Schaden ist, wer beteiligt ist und wann er auftritt. Durch die Trennung der Schadenscharakterisierung von Interventionsentscheidungen können Sicherheitsrichtlinien über explizite, von Klinikerinnen und Klinikern kuratierte Anweisungen außerhalb der Modellgewichte festgelegt werden.

Zur Skalierung der Annotation validierte das Team ein Gremium von LLM-Schiedsrichtern und trainierte MindGuard2 durch überwachtes Fine-Tuning auf kurzen Argumentationsspuren, gefolgt von Reinforcement Learning mit einer Strafe für die Argumentationslänge. Dies minimiert den Inferenzaufwand bei gleichzeitiger Beibehaltung der analytischen Vorteile.

In Tests mit öffentlichen Benchmarks und realen Gesprächen erzielt MindGuard2 niedrige Falsch-Positiv-Raten bei hohem Recall und hilft so, das Erkennen von Risiken mit dem Risiko unnötiger Interventionen auszubalancieren.
de.context: Die Verbreitung von Sprachmodellen im Bereich der psychischen Gesundheit erfordert robuste Schutzmechanismen, die Risiken präzise erkennen, ohne unzulässige Rechenverzögerungen zu verursachen oder das Vertrauen der Nutzer zu gefährden.
key_takeaways: Klinisch fundierte Taxonomie nach Was, Wer und Wann.
MindGuard2 bietet GLM-5.3-vergleichbare Leistung bei ca. 10-fach geringerer Latenz.
Niedrige Falsch-Positiv-Rate bei hohem Recall zum Schutz des Nutzervertrauens.
highlights: Entkopplung von Schadenscharakterisierung und Interventionsregeln durch externe Anweisungen.
Training mittels überwachtem Fine-Tuning und Reinforcement Learning mit Längestrafen.

items.title: Certify What You Plant: Shortcut-Free Proof Depth in Logical Reasoning Data
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33303v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Procedurally generated logic problems are used to both evaluate and train reasoning in language models. Their difficulty is usually set by planting a proof, that is, by sampling a proof of the desired depth and stating its premises as the problem. However, a planted proof is only one possible proof. A problem can also have shorter proofs, or several unrelated ones, and its stated depth then overstates what solving it requires. We measure what a problem actually requires, relative to a stated set of inference rules. For each problem, we compute the steps every proof must make, the shortest proof, the number of minimal proofs and the indispensable premises, and export certificates that an independent checker verifies. Audits of eight datasets find depth that is forced (ProofWriter, Blocksworld), problems labelled depth 5 that require about two specific rule applications (FLDx2), and answers that need no particular step (ZebraLogic). We then construct problems whose every proof has a requested structure, using a catalog of shortcuts proved once per rule set. Every constructed problem is checked in full and comes with its own certificate. In training, the best data mixes depths and problem types. At equal size, such mixtures of certified problem types, including model-checking problems that forward generation does not produce, transfer better than FLDx2-style derivation data for Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 8B.

items.title: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis in Jacobian-Space: Language and Vision Models Agree Approximately Up to a Rotation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33304v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) posits that AI models converge toward a shared representation of the world, even when trained on different data modalities. Previous work has found evidence for the PRH in the activations of vision and language models. In this work, we ask whether vision and language models also converge in how they act on these representations: precisely, in how these internal representations affect the models' output. At a chosen layer of a transformer, the Jacobian lens gives every word in the vocabulary (or class in an image classifier) a vector in the hidden state: the vector that most increases the model's tendency to generate that word, at that position or later, or to predict that class. Collectively, these vectors make up what is referred to as the model's J-space. We find evidence of the PRH in J-space across vision and language models, and furthermore, we find that J-spaces mostly converge up to a rotation. That is, a single rotation, fitted on a subset of words, approximately maps one model's J-space onto another's, and so applies to words and classes it was not fitted on. A word's vector, rotated from a text-only language model's J-space into the visual patch tokens of a vision-language model, changes the object the vision-language model says is in the image (and only in the image region where it is added). Rotated into an image generator's text conditioning, a word's vector changes the object in the generated image. Rotated into an ImageNet classifier (trained without text), it raises that object's class score above almost all others, and vice versa. This suggests that models converge not only in how they represent the world, but also in how they act on it.

items.title: Brand Recall and Category Accuracy in Language Models: An Audit of 1,000 B2B SaaS Brands
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33322v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A language model can name a brand without classifying it correctly. This study measures these outcomes separately for 1,000 B2B SaaS brands across 333 product categories. On Gemma 4 12B, with no external retrieval, category prompts elicit 510 brands (51.0%). A separate five-candidate category probe ranks the reference label first for 787 brands, a distractor first for 194, and yields little separation for 19. Among the 981 separated rankings, the error rate is 19.8%. It falls to 3.5% for the 547 brands with a winner-to-runner-up log-probability margin above 0.6. These are within-cohort measurements, not calibrated confidence estimates. Exploratory regressions associate technical coverage with recall and an owned-properties composite with category accuracy, but the composites use different adjustment sets and do not establish causal effects. Across four Gemma generations, measured recall is 39.8%, 44.3%, 51.1% and 51.0%. A separate representation-based sentiment measure has little linear association with customer ratings (r=0.03, n=921). The findings support reporting recall and category accuracy separately. Failure to elicit a brand does not establish its absence from model parameters or training data.

items.title: Confidence scores for gated automation of large language models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33394v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong capabilities in automated decision-making. However, LLMs may produce incorrect answers with high confidence, limiting their applicability in decisions that affect individuals and organizations. Reliable confidence scores are necessary to gate such decisions, and existing estimates are frequently unavailable or too coarse to support effective gating. This work uses supervised learning to train models to predict the correctness of LLM-generated answers, enabling automated confident responses and routing uncertain ones for human review. A linear confidence score head is fitted to the final-layer hidden state of the frozen LLM backbone, and text-only metamodels are trained as an alternative for closed models. All results come from a single 2B-parameter backbone, on graded answers that are about 98% SQuAD and the remainder TruthfulQA. Against multiple baselines, the confidence score head outperforms all baselines and metamodels, automating the largest fraction of the workload at high accuracy targets. Prompted confidence scores can appear well calibrated yet lack the resolution needed for thresholding. Although transferability to unseen datasets is modest, the confidence score head remains the most robust approach. The proposed confidence scoring framework enhances the safety of automating LLM-based agents and can be adapted to gate other properties, including safety or compliance.

items.title: Partial Routing: Trace-Tuned Delegation for Resource-Efficient Agentic Workflows
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33402v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI models vary enormously in capability and price. Model routing exploits this by sending easier tasks to cheaper models. However, a single agentic task often combines easy and difficult subtasks, making one model choice for the entire task inefficient. We introduce partial routing, which guides a frontier lead model to delegate suitable subtasks to a cheaper worker model. From both models' past runs, we identify recurring subtasks and measure each model's quality and cost on them. These measurements produce delegation guidance, with a parameter, $\delta$, controlling how much is delegated. The lead decides when and what to delegate during execution, without training either model. On held-out tasks from ViBench and Terminal-Bench 4.0, partial routing achieves higher mean task performance than the lead alone and task-level routing. With $\delta = 0.75$, it raises the lead's ViBench score from 70.2 to 78.5 at 19% lower cost, and its Terminal-Bench pass rate from 54% to 61% at similar cost. Giving the lead only the subtask breakdown, without a worker, also reduces cost on both benchmarks and raises the Terminal-Bench pass rate. These results show that analysis of past runs can support more efficient planning and more effective delegation, with little cost and implementation overhead.

items.title: Collaborative Language Models for Semantic IoT Data Processing: Validation through Zero-Shot Human Activity Recognition
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33411v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) systems generate low-level sensor observations that are not directly suitable for process analysis and must first be transformed into semantically meaningful events. This paper investigates collaborative language models as a zero-shot semantic abstraction layer for converting such observations into higher-level event and activity labels. We propose a five-stage workflow comprising semantic mapping, semantic aggregation, temporal and contextual aggregation, specialized reasoning, and final event abstraction. The resulting labels and contextual information can subsequently be represented as event records for downstream Process Mining (PM) tasks. The approach is evaluated through Human Activity Recognition on the CASAS Aruba smart home dataset using eleven workflow configurations. The experiments show that collaboration alone does not guarantee improved performance: general-purpose auxiliary SLMs can degrade recognition, whereas assigning complementary specialist roles leads to better results and allows a smaller final classifier to retain much of the performance of a larger model. The selected workflow achieves a macro F1 of 0.643 in the 1.5-day comparison and 0.567 (weighted F1 0.680) in a one-week evaluation. Although trained ML approaches remain more accurate on this dataset, the results demonstrate a different design point: modular semantic event abstraction using off-the-shelf models without task-specific parameter fine-tuning. The findings indicate that the structure of LM collaboration and task decomposition is more important than simply increasing the number of participating models.

items.title: Dynamic Reasoning in Next-Gen Detection and Response: An Empirical Study of LLM Triage, Reinforcement Tuning, and Adversarial Evasion
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33470v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present an end-to-end empirical study of dynamic reasoning in next-generation detection and response pipelines, evaluating how static classifiers, graph-based signal fusion, and large language model (LLM) triage agents perform under strict human-analyst attention budgets (Recall at B alerts/day). Across 56 reproducible experiments spanning a multi-layer enterprise-and-cloud simulator and four public datasets (SOREL-20M, BODMAS, LANL, and DARPA Transparent Computing), we test twelve architectural claims governing modern fleet-scale defense. First, we show that fleet growth halves recall at a fixed analyst budget even at negligible compute cost (<$0.0003 per million events), and that rarity-weighted graph risk propagation outperforms GraphSAGE without neural training. Second, evaluating frontier reasoning models (Gemini) and fine-tuned open-weight models (Qwen3-4B) for alert triage reveals that unconstrained LLM auto-closure eliminates 90% of false positives while silently discarding 31-44% of true attack cases. Third, post-training with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) causes severe reward hacking on unseen attack classes, suppressing up to 86% of novel attacks compared to two-epoch supervised fine-tuning. Finally, against an adaptive adversary generating plausible cover stories in benign telemetry fields, LLM triage evasion rises sharply unless gated by a deterministic policy harness prior to model invocation.

items.title: CA-RAG: Constraint-Aligned Retrieval for Structurally Faithful Long-Form Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33497v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically optimises evidence selection for semantic relevance, whereas compliance-sensitive long-form generation also requires evidence supporting explicit structural obligations. Semantically relevant retrieval may therefore omit information needed for mandatory downstream clauses. We propose Constraint-Aligned RAG (CA-RAG), a retrieval-conditioning framework that augments section-specific queries with ontology-derived structural constraints and policy-grounded knowledge-graph relations before evidence selection. Retrieval-only evaluation with manually annotated evidence shows consistent improvements across retrieval budgets. At $k=6$, CA-RAG increases Precision@$k$ from $0.5268$ to $0.5692$, pooled Recall@$k$ from $0.5402$ to $0.5950$, and F1@$k$ from $0.5389$ to $0.5672$ over standard RAG. Generation experiments further show improvements in compliance and reliability in several model--domain settings, while generation-only constraints achieve higher clause coverage but lower overall compliance and reliability. These results indicate that structurally aligned retrieval can improve evidence sufficiency in compliance-sensitive long-form generation.

items.title: Learning to Reason in Real-Time
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents that operate in the real world must reason correctly and on-time, yet they currently do not account for how time should alter their reasoning. Modern agents learn to do tasks in environments that are entirely synchronous: where the world waits for the agent to act before changing. A real-time environment, by contrast, changes independent of the agent. Existing approaches try to bridge this gap by imposing a ratio of thinking to acting. However, for an agent to succeed in real-time it must learn to act quickly when delay is costly and to reason longer when the benefit outweighs the missed opportunities. To this end, we introduce real-time reasoning training (RRT) as the class of training techniques for real-time reasoning agents. We develop three standard RRT techniques: (1) using real-time data, (2) decoupling acting and observing, and (3) curriculum learning in time. Together, these simple techniques substantially outperform strong baselines. Across time pressures, we outperform the strongest non-RRT baseline by an average of 33% reward on in-distribution and 55% reward on out-of-distribution tasks in two real-time environments: Frogger and Snake. These results demonstrate that we can teach agents to balance reasoning and responsiveness under real-time constraints, and that RRT opens a broad, new set of capabilities for real-time agents.

items.title: PeerReveal: Learning to Generalize in AI Peer Review Detection
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33555v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can we distinguish fully AI-generated reviews from those using AI only to rewrite human judgement? Furthermore, can we do so reliably when reviews are generated from diverse AI models and workflows across scientific domains? To this end, we introduce PeerReveal, a new detector that grounds its decisions in learned relationships between a review's claims and reference claims drawn from AI-generated reviews of the same paper, complemented by review-level textual signals. We evaluate PeerReveal on PeerShift, a new, challenging test set of 5,430 reviews spanning multiple domains, including machine learning, life sciences, and social sciences, combining variation in disciplinary review conventions with diverse AI review-production mechanisms. With regular training, PeerReveal achieves 70.52% pooled Macro-F1 on this benchmark, improving over the strongest baseline by 11.48 points. We develop an effective and practical adversarial training framework that further improves the detector's generalization using a small local generator optimized to produce challenging reviews, raising pooled Macro-F1 from 70.52% to 82.40%. These results show that robust AI-review detection benefits from richer review-level evidence and adversarial training on more challenging generation processes.

items.title: FIG-MAC: A Fine-grained Inspiration Graph Empowered Multi-Agent Collaboration for Automated Scientific Hypothesis Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33563v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated Scientific Hypothesis Generation (ASHG) leveraging large language models (LLMs) aims to harness their strengths in knowledge integration, logical reasoning, and text generation for efficiently producing innovative, verifiable scientific hypotheses. However, existing approaches face three critical limitations: (i) insufficient fine-grained knowledge representation, as unstructured context impairs LLM comprehension and reasoning; (ii) lack of knowledge evolution traceability, constraining the generation of innovative cross-domain conjectures; (iii) absence of human-inspired and role-specialized multi-agent collaboration, failing to leverage the efficient innovation mechanisms arising from cognitive diversity and division of labor among expert roles to complete the full ASHG-evaluation loop. To address these limitations, we propose the Fine-grained Inspiration Graph-empowered Multi-Agent Collaboration framework (FIG-MAC) including: (i) Fine-grained Inspiration Graph module (FIG), to obtain fine-grained structured knowledge representations, where nodes represent academic semantic units and edges encode heuristic relationships among them; (ii) ontology-guided hybrid reasoning module, which follows the FIG ontology to construct structured reasoning paths and uses vector search to enrich them with semantic evidence, to obtain the traceable scientific conjecture paths; (iii) role-specialized Multi-Agent framework, inspired by real scientific teamwork, enabling a closed-loop process of scientific conjecture generation, screening, and validation. Experimental results demonstrate that FIG-MAC significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on source diversity, provenance-adjusted novelty, and raw novelty.

items.title: Aligned Machine: A Benchmark for Evaluating Multimodal Embedding Similarity via Human Comparative Judgements
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33594v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Embedding models increasingly inform how people search, recommend, and retrieve information, yet we lack credible ways to test whether these similarity judgments reflect how humans understand meaning. Existing benchmarks typically rely on static, expert-labeled pairs with coarse Likert-style annotations, limiting scalability and making it difficult to obtain consistent, high-confidence annotations. We introduce Aligned Machine, an interactive, public-facing platform that transforms broad participation into a continuously growing Human-Aligned Similarity Benchmark (HASB) for evaluating semantic alignment in embedding-based systems. Participants complete a cognitively-natural, forced-choice task, comparing two pairs of items (text or images) and selecting which pair is more similar. This comparative design is accessible to non-experts, yields clean preference data, and supports robust aggregation. We report results from an initial deployment with 115 participants contributing 2,875 total labeled pairs and 872 unique pairs. Using HASB, we evaluated 12 widely used embedding models and found only partial alignment between embedding similarity and human judgments. Text-only models consistently achieve higher overall agreement than multimodal models, while multimodal performance varies systematically by task type: alignment is strongest for image-image comparisons, weaker for image-text comparisons, and lowest for text-text comparisons. Aligned Machine is designed to evolve over time as participation grows, supporting longitudinal analysis, domain-specific studies, bias detection, and measurement of concept drift across model versions.
