items.title: Learning from Natural Images Untangles Number Sense
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Numerical cognition is a simple yet fundamental ability that remains challenging for modern vision-language models. Meanwhile, number sense is already present in numerically na\"ive animals, suggesting that it can emerge without explicit numerical learning. Deep neural networks provide a related observation, with numerosity-selective units appearing after training on unrelated natural-image tasks and even before any training. However, these findings leave unresolved whether visual learning contributes beyond the spontaneous emergence of numerical selectivity. Human development provides a clue, as children become better at making judgments in which numerosity and proportion conflict. Here, we introduce a geometric framework to trace how representations of these two quantities change across learning. Although untrained and pretrained networks exhibited similar unit-level numerosity selectivity and basic comparison performance, natural-image pretraining increased the angle between numerosity and proportion subspaces while reducing their overlap, supporting more robust readout under conflict. Direct manipulation of these geometric properties further demonstrated their functional contributions to decoding accuracy and functional independence. Importantly, conventional supervised pretraining was not essential for quantity separation, which also emerged through self-supervised learning without category labels and synthetic-image training without natural-image exposure. Together, our findings suggest that structured visual learning can refine spontaneously emerging number sense into robust and functionally independent quantity representations without explicit numerical training.

items.title: Controllable CAD Generation and Interactive Editing of Fluid Rotors
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33617v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computer-aided design (CAD) provides the geometric foundation for rotors in fluid rotating machinery. However, creating models for different rotors requires different modeling processes, making it difficult to control geometry through design intent and reuse existing models. We introduce VaneCraft, an agent-driven framework for rotor generation, inverse recovery, and editing through a unified analytical representation. The agent interprets design requests and invokes geometric modeling operations. The representation defines geometric controls through meridional geometry and independent boundary angle laws. An anisotropic partial differential equation (PDE) maps these controls to the blade surfaces. Geometric parameter correction (GPC) uses a joint geometric encoder and a parameter decoder to refine controls initialized from rotor category and dimensions. Inverse recovery maps existing CAD to the same geometric controls for reconstruction and continued editing. Experiments demonstrate that VaneCraft supports anisotropy control and parameter editing and outperforms representative baselines in rotor CAD generation tasks. Project page is available on \href{https://github.com/shenchen333/vanecraft}{GitHub}.

items.title: How Much Effort Does an AI Code Reviewer Need? Evidence from Claude 5.5 Models on Plausible-but-Wrong Patches
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI coding agents write code faster than people can review it, so teams add AI reviewers. Reasoning models let such a reviewer trade cost for diligence through an effort setting. We asked how much effort a reviewer needs to catch plausible-but-wrong patches, which pass a benchmark's tests but fail stronger ones. Claude Opus 5.5 (preregistered), Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 (exploratory) each reviewed the same 90 agent-written Django patches from SWE-bench Verified at low, medium and high effort. By strengthened SWE-ABS tests, 55 patches were wrong and 35 correct. In every model, high effort accepted fewer wrong patches than low (false success .45 against .67 for Opus, .49 against .65 for Sonnet, .51 against .78 for Haiku), a supported difference for Opus and Haiku. For Opus, medium was non-inferior to high within 15 percentage points (difference .018, 95% CI [-.065, .108]) and cost 20% less, short of the preregistered 30%. For Sonnet and Haiku, medium cost 39% and 51% less than high but was not shown non-inferior. Opus at medium or high agreed best with the labels; Haiku at high cost about 8% as much per review as Opus at medium, accuracy difference unresolved. Exploratory coding showed that most rejections named the tested defect and that effort added such rejections. No setting is a strong gate: each accepted at least 45% of wrong patches. For 32 of the 55 wrong patches the issue may not require what the failing test checks; without them, neither accuracy hypothesis holds for any model.

items.title: SlicePlanner: Logic-Guided Agentic AI for Online QoS-Aware Network Slicing in Open RAN
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33664v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adaptive network slicing in Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) demands reconfiguration decisions that respond to live traffic conditions while remaining safe with respect to Service Level Agreement (SLA) constraints, a combination that purely data-driven controllers cannot reliably guarantee without continuous retraining. We present SlicePlanner, a logic-guided closed-loop framework that treats each RAN reconfiguration as a controlled hypothesis: proposed from live and historical KeyPerformance Indicator (KPI) evidence, filtered through explicit SLA constraints and mined RAN control rules, and committed only when post-action measurements confirm improvement. SlicePlanner comprises two cooperating agents: SliceSense, which monitors live KPIs, retrieves context-conditioned evidence, and ranks candidate RAN actions through a surrogate-guided admissibility filter; and SliceGuard, which validates post-action KPI responses, rolls back harmful configurations, and refreshes rules under distribution drift. Validated over the air using OpenAirInterface, FlexRIC, and commercial Sierra Wireless 5G devices, SlicePlanner reduces SLA latency violations by up to 86% over static slicing and 50% over Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL)-based slicing, while maintaining comparable cell throughput and auditable decisions without online retraining.

items.title: Interactive Proofs as a Unified Framework for Evaluating and Leveraging Verifiable Proof Generation by LLM Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33676v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in LLM-assisted theorem proving and program verification have attracted widespread attention. Beyond determining whether a proposition is true, LLM agents must produce evidence that can be independently checked by humans or formal verification tools. To evaluate the underlying, protocol-agnostic ability of LLM agents to construct verifiable proofs-rather than their proficiency with any particular proof language or verification tool, we introduce Merlin-Bench. Drawing on interactive proof systems from computational complexity theory, we cast an LLM agent as the prover: under a designated protocol, the agent interacts with a formal verifier to substantiate its claimed answer to a problem instance. We develop an automated framework for constructing test cases and use it to create 100 cases across 15 problem families, each formulated within this prover-verifier framework. Experiments with 10 frontier LLMs across multiple agent harnesses show that reliably producing verifiable proofs in accordance with specified protocols remains a substantial challenge. Our case studies further provide actionable insights into improving agents' ability to generate verifier-accepted proofs: tool use is essential for completing practical proof tasks; different forms of guidance, ranging from engineering instructions to problem-specific knowledge, substantially affect success rates on interactive-proof tasks; and proof-solving experience distilled from abstract tasks can transfer to concrete, real-world verification tasks.

items.title: Faster and Better Query (FBQ): Learning Future-Position Probes from the First Generated Token
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33679v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a large language model (LLM) evicts prompt keys and values at the end of prefill, it must decide what to keep before it sees the queries from subsequent decoding steps. Generating a draft continuation can approximate those queries at the cost of extra autoregressive steps. Can we use the embedding of the first output token, already available from the final prefill logits, to construct low-cost pseudo queries that approximate future decoding queries? We start with FTQ-8, which places eight copies of the first token ID at consecutive future positions and reads their attention to the prompt in one causal forward pass. Each copy sees a different prefix, but a generic opening such as the offers a poor literal guess for seven successive tokens. Faster and Better Query (FBQ) preserves the first embedding and learns an additive offset at each of the seven remaining positions. We train these offsets to predict the average prompt attention of a full-cache continuation. On LongBench, FBQ performs comparably to eight-step Lookahead Q-Cache at the same cache budget, using a single forward pass to compute all probe queries.

items.title: EVA: Evidence-seeking Visual Agent for Hallucination-Resistant Multimodal Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33706v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hallucinations in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often arise from visual assumptions that go unchecked. Self-reflection, multi-agent debate, and counterfactual verification can reinforce erroneous conclusions when they rely on the same unverified visual assumptions. External visual tools can provide verifiable evidence, but models may select the wrong tools, supply incorrect parameters, or ignore or contradict the evidence they obtain. In this work, we propose EVA, an Evidence-seeking Visual Agent that reframes multimodal reasoning as an explicit process of evidence acquisition and verification. At the core of EVA is a unified evidence-grounded execution pipeline designed to address the above challenges through two tightly coupled mechanisms. First, we introduce Iterative Tool Replanning, which dynamically refines tool selection and parameters based on intermediate observations, improving the reliability of tool usage. Second, we develop Evidence Consistency Verification, an answer validation mechanism that improves alignment between the final prediction and the collected evidence, mitigating evidence--reasoning inconsistencies. In addition, to balance robustness and efficiency, EVA incorporates Selective Evidence Routing, an adaptive fast--slow reasoning strategy that determines when external evidence is necessary. Visually straightforward queries are handled via direct reasoning, while complex or high-risk cases trigger tool-based evidence acquisition. By jointly addressing how to reliably acquire evidence and how to use it consistently, EVA transforms multimodal reasoning from passive answer validation into explicit evidence-backed decision making. Experimental results demonstrate that EVA achieves significant

items.title: P-FedSkill: A Personalized Federated Skill Learning Framework under Task Heterogeneity
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33707v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Skill learning has become an important way to improve agent performance. However, agent trajectories often contain sensitive information and cannot be shared across clients, hindering collaborative skill learning. To tackle this issue, federated skill learning (FSL) has emerged as a solution by distilling trajectories into compact skill representations and uploading them to a central server for sharing. However, existing FSL methods typically share skills based on skill similarity without considering their contributions to heterogeneous tasks across clients, thereby degrading agent performance. To address this challenge, we propose P-FedSkill, a personalized FSL framework that comprises three key components: local skill extraction (LSE), personalized skill selection (PSS), and task-aware skill routing (TASR). Specifically, LSE first extracts skill patches (i.e., task applicability conditions and execution strategies) and task execution outcomes from trajectories. PSS then uses these outcomes to evaluate each skill patch's performance on client tasks and incorporates its task applicability condition to construct a personalized skill set for each client. Finally, TASR adaptively selects a task-relevant subset of skill patches based on their applicability conditions to guide agent execution. We further provide a theoretical guarantee for personalized skill selection in P-FedSkill, and extensive experiments also demonstrate its effectiveness.

items.title: PowerFix: Physics-Guided Iterative Repair for LLM-Assisted Power Converter Design
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly being explored for automated engineering design. However, repairing power-converter designs that fail engineering validation remains challenging: the system must identify physical causes, locate responsible design variables, and resolve violations without compromising other constraints. We introduce PowerFix, a physics-guided iterative repair framework that converts validation failures into structured diagnoses and executable patches while preserving topology and design requirements. PowerDiagGraph links failed checks to possible physical causes and constrains repair routes. An LLM prioritizes these routes, while a deterministic compiler translates selected repairs into authorized field-level edits. Candidates are validated on isolated design copies and committed only after all required engineering checks pass; failed validation can guide replanning. On our constructed 96-task flyback repair benchmark, comprising injected single faults, coupled faults, and held-out natural failures from our design generator, PowerFix achieves 78.7% verified repair success rate (VRSR), compared with 30.1% for the strongest of three LLM baselines. Three additional replanning rounds increase VRSR to 88.4%. These offline results provide pilot-stage evidence within a simulation-based design workflow, with hardware prototype validation and transfer to a second converter topology as the next steps toward deployment.

items.title: KeyDeck: Multi-Paper-to-Slide Generation via Cross-Paper Synthesis and Reference-Guided Personalization
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33715v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-paper-to-slide generation (multi-PTSG) is the task of constructing a unified presentation from multiple research papers by selecting, organizing, and synthesizing information across sources. This task introduces two main challenges: (i) combining multiple sources into a coherent narrative requires identifying cross-paper relationships and synthesizing their content, and (ii) the desired organization and emphasis varies substantially across presenters, making personalization essential for user satisfaction. Motivated by these challenges, we propose KeyDeck, the first multi-PTSG framework that integrates per-paper and cross-paper analysis to identify relationships among sources and synthesize their contributions into a coherent narrative, and reference-guided personalization to infer presenters' narrative, content, textual, and visual preferences and adapt slide generation accordingly. To evaluate generation quality, personalization adherence, and conversational goal satisfaction, we introduce KeyBench, a benchmark of 100 expert-authored multi-paper presentations, together with a comprehensive evaluation framework. Our results demonstrate that KeyDeck outperforms existing approaches in multi-PTSG quality, personalization adherence, and conversational goal satisfaction.

items.title: Asset4D-Bench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Editable 3D and 4D Reconstruction
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33728v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A cart can follow its reference trajectory while its cargo floats above the deck. Asset4D-Bench tests whether coding agents recover objects, motion and interactions from visual references as editable Blender scenes. Its 114 conditions span image editing, video reconstruction with matched full or partial starter assets, and independently selected from-scratch tasks. We independently reopen projects and measure them against native reference states. The 228 archived scores include original delivery outcomes and versioned measures of scene quality. On 24 from-scratch tasks, each model earns full dynamics credit on 14. Of these, three GPT-6.1-Sol and eight GPT-6-Astra reconstructions earn zero relation points. Under the fixed scoring weights, relations contribute 5.15 points to the 6.50-point Sol-minus-Astra difference in mean recovered fidelity. Differences in execution and recovery policy across archived runs preclude a causal estimate of starter-asset effects.

items.title: JOVE ICE: Intent Guided Cloud Edge Device Collaboration for AI Glasses
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33735v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and LLM based agents have expanded the capabilities of AI glasses, enabling egocentric visual question answering, memory retrieval, and proactive assistance. These applications involve diverse inputs, including speech, images, and video, and range from simple device control to complex visual reasoning, posing challenges for efficient computation and communication. While video centric capabilities have received considerable attention, simple text based and device executable tasks remain underexplored despite their prevalence in daily interactions. Efficiently supporting diverse workloads within a unified assistant remains an open challenge. We propose JOVE ICE, an intent guided cloud, edge, and device collaborative framework that routes requests among AI glasses, a paired smartphone, and cloud servers according to user intent. JOVE ICE integrates hierarchical intent classification with dynamic subagent orchestration to select efficient execution paths and flexibly incorporate new applications through specialized subagents. Analysis of real world AI glasses requests reveals that simple device control tasks account for over 30% of interactions, which JOVE ICE handles directly on device to avoid unnecessary cloud computation and costs. Evaluations on three public benchmarks demonstrate that JOVE ICE reduces time to first token by approximately 13% and token usage by over 11% compared with conventional device and cloud architectures, while maintaining task quality. These results demonstrate the potential of intent guided collaboration to improve the efficiency and scalability of AI glasses.

items.title: WhatIf: Counterfactual World Models over Action-Grounded Causal Graphs for Robotic Manipulation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33745v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: World models predict what happens under an action, but choosing between actions requires comparing their outcomes in the same physical situation. Factual transitions alone determine action-wise marginal futures and average effects, but not individual effects or the probability that switching actions causes harm. We introduce WhatIf, a counterfactual world model for manipulation that couples candidate futures through shared latent physics and transition noise inferred from factual history. Each candidate action induces a sparse object-factor causal graph describing the physical pathways it activates. Rolling out these graphs under the shared situation anchors predictions to observed outcomes and confines action contrasts to the objects each action reaches. Shared type-conditioned functions support varying numbers of objects, while a round-trip loss enforces action-invariant abduction without counterfactual labels. We show that replacing an individual effect with its conditional mean incurs mean-squared error equal to its conditional variance, motivating comparisons between coupled futures. Building on these comparisons, Counterfactual Advantage Planning (CAP) ranks plans by their advantage over an incumbent within shared situations and constrains the probability of harm. Paired advantages reduce estimator variance by a factor of $1-\rho$, where $\rho$ is the correlation between branch outcomes, and cancel model errors shared by both branches. Each executed transition provides hindsight advantages to update the physics posterior, the next plan, and an amortized policy without a learned critic. We further establish when observational transitions identify interventional dynamics. Paired simulator interventions evaluate counter

items.title: REFORGE: LLM-Assisted RTL Bug Repair with Structured Context and Verification Feedback
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33748v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can write and repair RTL, but successful compilation or testbench execution does not establish defect removal, behavioral preservation, security, or implementation feasibility. Existing LLM-based RTL repair methods often report a single repair rate without retaining separate evidence for these properties, limiting reproducible comparison and integration into hardware design flows. We present REFORGE, which, to our knowledge, is the first LLM-assisted RTL repair framework that maintains and accumulates structured repair evidence across iterations, allowing it to generate fixes that satisfy multiple objectives simultaneously, including functionality, behavioral equivalence, security, and cost efficiency. REFORGE profiles buggy RTL, identifies structural and security-relevant features, localizes failing behavior, and uses verification-guided diagnosis to generate complete RTL repair variants. Each variant undergoes syntax checking, simulation, formal analysis, off-trigger preservation, security re-scan, and synthesis-based power, performance, and area analysis. We implement REFORGE as a backend-independent repair-and-verification flow and evaluate it in 288 runs across three LLM backends and three benchmark suites. On CirFix, the proposed context and diagnosis increase runs delivering a checked repair from 32/63 to 51/63, while every configuration repairs the Hack@DAC OpenTitan defect. Evidence records also show that a testbench-only criterion reports 3.9 times more repairs than the full set of applicable checks, security-clean outputs may lack functional verification, and different RTL repairs can implement equivalent hardware. These results show that LLM-generated RTL repairs require explicit mu

items.title: TransHarness: From Benchmark Overfitting to Transferable Harness Evolution
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33757v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Harness evolution offers a path to improving coding agents without updating model weights. However, existing methods can overfit their evolution benchmarks, producing gains that fail to carry over to new tasks. To address this challenge, we introduce Transferable Harness Evolution (TransHarness), which evolves harness intervention policies from same-task success-failure contrasts. These policies couple execution-context triggers with diagnostic guidance, enabling task-dependent checks and corrections beyond the source executions. Cross-task replay and independent semantic selection retain policies that intervene selectively and ground corrections in current-task evidence rather than source-specific solutions. We further curate an independent evolution set for cross-distribution transfer and conduct a cross-benchmark evaluation covering multiple strong models and a range of lightweight and mature harnesses. Experiments show that, with only 300 source trajectories from outside the test distribution, TransHarness further improves strong agents across distinct target benchmarks, demonstrating transferable harness evolution beyond benchmark overfitting. Specifically, TransHarness achieves state-of-the-art scores of 76.4% on DeepSWE v1.1 and 95.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, surpassing the strongest baseline model, GPT-6 Astra, by 2.4 and 5.6 percentage points, respectively.

items.title: Improving Building Energy Efficiency with an Indoor Environmental World Model and Counterfactual Adaptive Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33764v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optimizing indoor climate systems plays a critical role in achieving the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals 11 and 13. However, indoor delayed thermodynamic responses and partial observability severely hinder existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods, which are primarily limited by implicit thermal inertia, occupancy dynamic prediction, and cumulative prediction errors during long-horizon rollouts. Thus, we propose a novel occupant-centric indoor climate control framework. It develops indoor environmental world models to predict future physical thermal baselines and dynamic occupancy, explicitly capturing latent thermal inertia. By formulating adaptive regulation as counterfactual advantage learning against future environments via a Branching Dueling Q-Network, and integrating a Held-Action TD-{\lambda} target, it effectively mitigates delayed credit assignment. Additionally, a proposed physics-aligned smoothness regularization suppresses high-frequency actuator fluctuations, potentially extending equipment service life. Experiments on SemiBuildingSim and Sinergym demonstrate that our method achieves a superior multi-objective trade-off. Compared to the best-performing methods, it further reduces energy consumption by 11.2%, occupant discomfort by 44.2%, and action fluctuation by 47.3%, achieving better sample efficiency and cross-region effectiveness. This interdisciplinary study offers an energy-efficient, occupant-centric AI solution for control science, building science, and energy sustainability.

items.title: CHD-Bench: Diagnosing Congenital Heart Disease through Interactive Examination
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33775v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diagnosis of congenital heart disease (CHD) requires understanding the spatial relationships between cardiac structures, which clinicians assess by scrolling through CT or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) slices and rotating 3D reconstructions. Although automated methods have advanced cardiac segmentation, identifying congenital heart defects from volumetric scans remains an open challenge. The two existing approaches rely on handcrafted diagnostic rules limited to static anatomical abnormalities. We introduce CHD-Bench, the first benchmark for interactive CHD diagnosis, defining a multi-label task and evaluation protocol over 247 CT and MRI scans from three cohorts covering 38 CHD types. We also present CHD-Harness, open-source software that runs a VLM in a 3D Slicer environment through 22 tools, manages each examination, and records the resulting diagnosis and supporting views. We evaluate off-the-shelf medical, open weight, and closed weight VLMs and compare them with a 3D CNN classifier and published rule-based results. Gemini 4 Argon with CHD-Harness achieves the highest macro F1 across all three cohorts (0.63, 0.63, and 0.43). Allowing for interactive examination raises its macro F1 by up to 20 points over static views. These results establish CHD-Bench and CHD-Harness as a foundation for developing and evaluating VLMs for interactive CHD diagnosis.

items.title: InterGenEHR$^+$: An Interactive Framework for Natural Language-Conditioned Generation of Longitudinal Patient Trajectories
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33788v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Objective: To develop and validate InterGenEHR$^+$, an interactive framework for natural language-conditioned generation of synthetic tabular electronic health records (EHRs) and longitudinal trajectories for scenario-based evaluation of machine learning models. Methods: An optional large language model (LLM) parser converts clinical requests into structured constraints. Conditional variational autoencoders and diffusion models generate single-time-point records, while diffusion models generate longitudinal trajectories. We evaluate parsing, distributional fidelity, imputation, clinical-constraint adherence, mortality prediction, and clinical plausibility using a multi-institutional cohort of 874 patients receiving venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO). Results: Gemma 3 4B with few-shot prompting achieves the highest parsing performance with a low spurious slot rate. IGE-TabDDPM and IGE-PMVAE perform well in single-time-point generation; IGE-CSDI, IGE-FGTI, and IGE-MTSCI lead on different longitudinal fidelity metrics. Across five random seeds and three classifiers, synthetic cohorts retain predictive utility for mortality prediction on real test data. Clinician ratings support trajectory plausibility and alignment with requested scenarios. Conclusion: InterGenEHR$^+$ supports clinician-specified generation of EHR trajectories with statistical fidelity and downstream predictive utility in the evaluated VV-ECMO cohort. Extension to other clinical settings requires further validation. Significance: The framework supports scenario-based evaluation of machine learning models in data-sparse critical care settings.

items.title: ExtractBench Pro: The Long Tail of Document Extraction
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33791v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present ExtractBench Pro, a schema-guided document extraction benchmark that tests six challenging modes of extraction underrepresented in existing datasets. It is created following a framework for synthetic document generation, in which deterministic document generators assemble challenging components into documents that are designed to be difficult at a level calibrated for frontier systems. We synthesize 100 realistic documents spanning a diverse range of styles. On this data, we evaluate ten coding agents and eight extraction API configurations for accuracy, grounding, and their ability to perfectly extract documents. No extraction system extracts more than 61% of documents error-free. The strongest general-purpose coding agents, Claude Code Opus 5.5 and Codex GPT-6 Astra, outperform specialized extraction APIs on both perfect-document rate and Value F1, but at a higher cost per page. Among specialized extraction APIs, LlamaExtract spans the lower-cost frontier, with Agentic Plus Max Effort approaching the strongest coding agent on both perfect-document rate and Value F1 at lower cost per page. Our analysis of coding agent traces identifies intelligent image processing and programmatic reasoning, but also failures in applying document-specific definitions and recovering relationships from diagrams. We release ExtractBench Pro and these evaluation results as resources for the future development of improved frontier extraction systems.

items.title: Keep or Roll Back? Out-of-Loop Judges for Self-Improving VLA and End-to-End Embodied Policies
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33794v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-improvement is now a practical recipe for embodied policies: a policy collects experience, is retrained, and is kept when a judge rates it higher. However, the judge is usually trained or chosen inside the same loop, so its evidence is not independent of the policy. We introduce SealedLoop, an evaluation framework that adds a sealed judge: an evaluator outside the loop that the improver cannot see or optimize against. A new policy is kept only when a sequential test on the sealed judge confirms the gain, with a bounded probability of keeping a worse one. Running the same loop under each judge, we separate two sources of a false gain, which we call judge error (the loop's judge is wrong on its own data) and transfer gap (a real gain there does not carry over to unseen conditions). We evaluate on LIBERO manipulation, NAVSIM driving, and a full-scale real vehicle. In manipulation, a success classifier accepted 65 of 196 failures in one generation. In driving, policies that gain on the loop's own frames lose in an unseen city, so even an exact in-loop judge would keep 8/15 of them. When the sealed test decides, a driving loop built to improve ends with a better policy than under its own critic (0.674 against 0.649 PDMS, from 0.638), and on driving pairs with known sealed gain the test accepted 11 of 12 real gains and none of 59 losses. In a real-world field experiment on a published improvement step, the reinforced version drove further into a curve than the version it started from in all 6 blind pairs, though neither completed it. These results show that evidence from inside the loop, however accurate, is not enough to decide whether a policy has improved. SealedLoop offers a foundation for trustworthy self-improvement o

items.title: Ensuring Deployment-Time Safety of Neural Network Controlled Systems via Localized Certificate Repair
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33813v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Barrier certificates provide formal safety guarantees for neural network controlled systems by ensuring that system trajectories avoid unsafe regions over time. However, after deployment, previously unseen obstacles or constraint changes may introduce new unsafe regions, invalidating the original certificate and potentially leading to unsafe behavior. We address this setting with adaptive piecewise barrier certificates, which preserve the original certificate and policy in unchanged regions while introducing localized updates around newly emerged unsafe regions. The central question is how to perform such updates efficiently during system execution without retraining from scratch. Our key idea is to cast deployment-time adaptation as a localized certificate repair problem and reduce it to an optimization task that leverages the learned structure of previous barrier certificates, enabling fast updates without global retraining. We further design a staged repair framework that progressively transitions from localized repair to joint policy-certificate updates and, when necessary, localized retraining. Empirical results on four benchmarks with five new obstacles show that our method succeeds in all cases and completes within tens of seconds on average, whereas retraining from scratch fails in most cases. On instances where retraining succeeds, our method is 17.3$\times$ faster on average. It incurs only 16.2% performance degradation relative to the original policy.

items.title: Spectral Optimal Transport for Dynamics-Aware Sign Language Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33818v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sign language generation (SLG) translates spoken-language text into pose sequences that convey its meaning. Recently, flow-based models with optimal transport (OT) have become a strong SLG baseline by handling the one-to-many nature of text-to-sign. While classifier-free guidance (CFG) could be applied to further strengthen the semantic alignment theoretically, its training involves conditional and unconditional training, which may contradict the pose-space OT, thus reducing the generation quality. Under the condition dropout, one noise sample can be paired with target motions exhibiting incompatible motion dynamics, interfering with the semantic guidance when the text condition is present. To address this issue, we propose Spectral Optimal Transport (SOT), which augments the pose-space cost with a spectral feature distance, reweighting the coupling toward the temporal-frequency structure of the target motions, thereby improving the performance when using CFG. The quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

items.title: RadOncGym: An Agent-Based Framework for Radiotherapy Dose-Mimicking Optimization
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33821v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI dose-prediction models generate patient-specific 3D dose distributions from patient anatomy, providing an important intermediate representation for automated radiotherapy planning. However, an AI-predicted dose must undergo downstream optimization to produce a physically constrained treatment plan, a process that requires balancing competing planning objectives. We present RadOncGym, an agent-based framework that enables an LLM agent to iteratively tune 12 planning-objective weights for dose-mimicking optimization. To reduce iterative evaluation cost, RadOncGym incorporates a surrogate verifier that provides rapid feedback while allowing the agent to decide when to request a full planning solve within a fixed solve budget. We evaluate RadOncGym on 60 OpenKBP head-and-neck patients, each paired with 10 predictions from OpenKBP-Opt dose-prediction sets, yielding 600 patient-prediction contexts per experimental configuration. Under RadOncGym's 16-turn setting with a three-solve budget, a GPT-5.6 Sol agent reduces mean clinical-criterion violation by 0.6131 Gy and improves DVH and dose scores by 0.5986 and 0.2204 Gy relative to leaving all 12 weights fixed at 1, outperforming all evaluated non-agent weight-tuning methods under the same solve budget. It remains competitive with the 16-solve variants of these methods while requiring 75.0-77.6% less normalized runtime. RadOncGym demonstrates the potential of LLM agents as optimization planners in downstream radiotherapy plan optimization and provides a public testbed for their systematic evaluation. Code and configurations are available at https://github.com/miaot-usc/RadOncGym.

it.title: Come Clay sviluppa gli agenti GTM con Jeff Barg
it.summary: In questo episodio parliamo con Jeff Barg, Head of AI di Clay, per scoprire come la piattaforma punta a offrire risultati comparabili sia usando il proprio agente sia puntando Claude Code su Clay. L'utilizzo è già diviso quasi a metà tra l'agente proprietario e harness esterni.
it.why_it_matters: Comprendere come una piattaforma adotta harness esterni e agenti proprietari offre uno sguardo concreto sull'evoluzione degli strumenti di go-to-market nell'era dell'intelligenza artificiale.
it.extended_analysis:
Il panorama degli agenti di intelligenza artificiale si evolve rapidamente, e l'approccio di Clay offre spunti interessanti su come le piattaforme software gestiscono l'interazione tra strumenti interni e harness esterni come Claude Code. La suddivisione dell'utilizzo quasi al 50/50 evidenzia la flessibilità richiesta dagli sviluppatori e dagli utenti professionali.

Nel corso dell'episodio, Jeff Barg approfondisce le strategie e le scelte architetturali dietro la costruzione di agenti GTM (go-to-market). Ascoltando il podcast, i professionisti del settore possono esaminare da vicino le metriche d'uso reali e le sfide tecniche affrontate dal team.

Le implicazioni per il settore riguardano l'apertura degli ecosistemi software e la crescente importanza di interoperabilità e flessibilità nell'adozione degli agenti AI.
it.context: L'episodio esplora lo sviluppo degli agenti GTM da parte di Clay, esaminando l'adozione divisa tra agenti interni e strumenti esterni come Claude Code nel contesto attuale delle piattaforme AI.
key_takeaways: L'utilizzo della piattaforma è diviso quasi equamente tra l'agente di Clay e harness esterni.

en.title: How Clay Builds GTM Agents with Jeff Barg
en.summary: In this episode, we chat with Jeff Barg, Head of AI at Clay, to explore how the platform aims for comparable results whether using its own agent or pointing Claude Code at Clay. Usage is already split nearly 50/50 between Clay's agent and outside harnesses.
en.why_it_matters: Examining how a platform balances proprietary agents with external harnesses provides practical insight into the evolution of go-to-market AI tooling.
en.extended_analysis:
The AI agent landscape continues to shift, and Clay's approach sheds light on how software platforms handle the balance between proprietary systems and external harnesses like Claude Code. With usage split nearly 50/50, the conversation highlights the flexibility expected by modern developers and teams.

Jeff Barg discusses the architectural and strategic choices behind building GTM (go-to-market) agents. Listeners can expect to learn about real-world usage patterns and the technical considerations involved in scaling AI agents.

The broader implications point toward a future where interoperability and openness matter just as much as proprietary features in software ecosystems.

Humans in a Post-Human World
items.summary: I’ve spent more than forty years writing software. AI agents now write it better than I do. My daughter Athena is fourteen and earns straight A’s in high school. How do I help her choose a career when her AI study partner will likely do that work better than she can? Today those agents are my teammates, and I still decide what we’re trying to build. If machines eventually do all the work, where does that leave me? And who earns the money to buy what they make? As an AI and autonomy research engineer, I study how a swarm of machines can think and act as one in the physical world. That’s a form of distributed embodied intelligence. As a licensed wildlife rehabilitator, I’ve spent years caring for injured, ill, and orphaned animals. A raccoon’s fate can turn on whether the person who finds it sees a nuisance or a life worth saving. When a swarm of machines develops a conscious mind that can outthink us, we may learn what that encounter feels like from the raccoon’s side. I’m Chris Benson. This solo episode of Practical AI grew out of the questions I’m wrestling with as I write Humans in a Post-Human World . This Thanksgiving, I’m grateful I get to be Athena’s dad. She needs advice no one had to give me at fourteen. I want her to grow up as sure of her worth as I am, even if a machine can do everything on her résumé. What would you tell her? en.title: Humans in a Post-Human World: Navigating AI and Careers

Drawing from his background as an AI research engineer and parent, he examines what career guidance looks like when machines can outperform humans.
en.why_it_matters: As AI systems advance, we must rethink education, human worth, and career planning for the next generation in a rapidly changing technological landscape.
en.extended_analysis:
Chris Benson brings together decades of software engineering experience and observations on distributed embodied intelligence to question the trajectory of a post-human world. By comparing the potential rise of superintelligent machines to our historical interactions with the natural world, he poses profound ethical and philosophical questions.

The discussion challenges traditional educational paradigms and invites listeners to consider how humanity maintains economic security and personal value when automation replaces human labor across industries.
en.context: Rapid advancements in autonomous agents and AI-driven automation are forcing a critical evaluation of long-term economic structures, educational standards, and human purpose.
key_takeaways: AI agents can now outperform experienced developers in software creation tasks.
Traditional educational models may fail to prepare students for an AI-dominated workforce.
Distributed embodied intelligence presents new philosophical parallels for human-machine dynamics.

items.title: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite
items.summary: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite This additional SQLite tool has been around for a while now - it was added as "experimental" in SQLite 3.47.0 in October 2024 and enhanced in SQLite 3.50.0 in May 2025 . It was only today that I understood one of its most attractive characteristics. Normally, if you want to grab a snapshot copy of a SQLite database, you need to use either the backup API or VACUUM INTO . In both cases you need enough disk space to create a duplicate copy of your database, so if you're on a small instance and you already use more than half of the available disk you are plain out of luck. sqlite3_rsync can copy a snapshot of your database over an SSH connection to another machine, without first needing to create a full local copy! It's also good for synchronizing an existing copy of a database without re-transmitting the entire thing over the network. It works in a similar way to regular rsync: The core idea behind the protocol is that the replica sends cryptographic hashes for pages or groups of pages over to the origin side. The origin sends back page content that differs, or requests finer-grain hashes if a multi-page hash does not match. If the origin and replica start out being vastly different, the total network bandwidth can exceed the size of the entire database, due to the overhead of exchanging hashes, but the excess bandwidth is not great - a few percent at most. Update : Hah! Turns out I wrote about this application of sqlite_rsync back in October 2024 when the tool was first released. Tags: backups , sqlite

items.title: The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
items.summary: My comment on The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features — Hacker News. I had a NYT photographer take my picture at my home earlier this year (for a story about Moltbook, oddly enough). At one point I asked if they could fix things up if I had a stain on my shirt and they said absolutely not - they present photographs as they were taken, with cropping and balancing applied but no edits beyond that. He did spend a bunch of time trying to find the best possible natural lighting for the shots he wanted. The photo at the top of https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/02/technology/moltbook-ai-so... is my laptop, taken in my garden, after hunting around for the best spot that didn't have too much glare on the screen. You can see how dirty my screen is, too! Photography for a newspaper is photo journalism, and they take it seriously. (Thankfully I did not have a visible stain on my shirt.) it.title: La rivoluzione contro il Rinascimento dell'IA
it.summary: In questo episodio di Latent Space, Thariq Shihipar di OpenAI esplora come l'intelligenza artificiale possa rendere il software economico da produrre in massa, lasciando comunque il tempo per curare i dettagli di una singola creazione.
it.why_it_matters: Comprendere come produzione di massa e artigianato digitale possano coesistere offre una prospettiva cruciale sul futuro dello sviluppo software.
it.extended_analysis:
Registrato in occasione di AI Engineer CODE, l'intervento si concentra su come la tecnologia possa cambiare i paradigmi di creazione. Attraverso esempi pratici, come la modifica delle dimensioni di una roccia all'interno di un videogioco di combattimento, viene mostrato il potenziale concreto di questi strumenti.

Il podcast esamina due futuri apparentemente in conflitto: una rivoluzione basata sulla velocità e sulla quantità, e un Rinascimento focalizzato sul valore estetico e sulla cura artigianale. La discussione invita a riflettere su come bilanciare efficienza e qualità espressiva nel lavoro di sviluppo.
it.context: Il panorama dello sviluppo software sta evolvendo rapidamente grazie agli strumenti di intelligenza artificiale generativa, sollevando interrogativi su come cambieranno i flussi di lavoro e i ruoli professionali.
key_takeaways: L'IA può ridurre drasticamente i costi di produzione del software.
È possibile coniugare la scalabilità della produzione di massa con la cura artigianale del singolo dettaglio.
Esempi pratici, come lo sviluppo di videogiochi, illustrano la coesistenza di questi due futuri.

en.extended_analysis:
Recorded at AI Engineer CODE, the discussion highlights the dual potential of artificial intelligence to scale software production effortlessly while preserving the human touch needed to make specific elements feel right.

The episode juxtaposes a revolution of abundance with a renaissance of refined craftsmanship. By looking at practical demonstrations, listeners gain perspective on how developers might navigate these two competing futures in their daily work.
en.context: As generative AI tools reshape development pipelines, engineers and creators are actively exploring new balances between automated output quality and bespoke design.
key_takeaways: AI can enable the low-cost production of software by the thousand.
Automation can coexist with dedicated time for nuanced, single-item refinement.
Practical demonstrations from game development illustrate these concepts in action.

Coding agents in November 2025 Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5 . With hindsight, this was a consequential model. items.title: Building AI That Can Reason Under Uncertainty with Thore Graepel - #786
items.summary: In this episode, Thore Graepel, CEO and co-founder of Metis Reasoning and Chair of Machine Learning at UCL, joins us to explore an approach to AI reasoning inspired by his work on AlphaGo. We discuss why he believes reliable reasoning requires explicit representations of knowledge and uncertainty, with language models helping to generate hypotheses and interpret evidence. Thore explains how a system could break down complex questions, gather evidence, and choose its next step based on the uncertainty it expects to resolve. We examine how this differs from agent harnesses, where smaller models and decision models might fit, and how knowledge and reasoning strategies can improve independently. We also consider the difficult judgment calls involved in assessing evidence, handling conflicting sources, and avoiding overconfidence. Finally, we discuss the limits of answer-focused benchmarks and what it would take to evaluate whether a system’s reasoning genuinely supports its conclusions. 🗒️ Full show notes: ⁠⁠⁠https://twimlai.com/go/786.

it.title: Costruire un'IA che ragiona nell'incertezza con Thore Graepel

items.summary: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries: With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library . It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. Here's the digitized sketchbook . Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work. Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue ? Mark thinks it will be mild: But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. items.title: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
items.summary: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this: In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count. This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said: Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. GLM 5.4 is not yet available as open weights: We plan to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening. I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API. It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1 ), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model. I built a llm-glm plugin , then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because llm-zai doesn't yet support the new model, but I'll likely retire mine once that plugin catches up. Here are pelicans for GLM-5.4 on low, high, and max. items.title: Ladybird's first alpha release
items.summary: Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS . This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha , which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself! items.title: datasette-charts 0.1a0
items.summary: Release: datasette-charts 0.1a0 I've been thinking about this problem for over a year now, but on Sunday I finally fired up Claude Fable 5.2 to build an initial prototype. The prototype went so well that this is now a full plugin. You can try it out in Datasette Lite here . It looks like this: The new charts plugin works against any table or arbitrary SQL query in Datasette. It defines several different chart types (using vendored D3 , Observable Plot , and topojson-client ), each with a set of heuristics for identifying when they might be a good match for a specific set of rows. Those suggestion thumbnails at the top are actual visualizations driven by the data, and selecting one pulls up the full chart along with tools for modifying it. You can also manually construct a chart from scratch. As with other Datasette visualization plugins, the current state of your chart is persisted in a #fragment in the URL - so you can bookmark charts or share them with others. The most important feature is that the charts take all rows into account . Previous charting plugins like datasette-vega would only show charts for the current page of results, generally up to 100 rows. The new plugin compiles each chart to a SQL query that aggregates across the entire result set (potentially millions of rows) using GROUP BY, time bucketing, and window functions. Each query returns a result capped at 5,000 rows, suitable for display on the chart. The plugin uses sampling to help suggest charts for larger tables without evaluating the full result set. I'm really happy with this initial release of the plugin. It's still very much an alpha, but it's the closest I've got to the dream of Datasette helping visualize data with as little required direction from the user as possible. Tags: coding-agents

items.title: Muru
items.summary: Muru Graham Dumpleton started mod_wsgi 20 years ago, and has been thinking about the ideal way to serve Python web applications in production ever since. Muru is his new, AI-assisted Rust server that aims to provide the best possible tools for running ASGI and WSGI Python apps both in development and production. As he did with wrapture , he's been publishing an extraordinarily detailed account of the project as he works on it - as part of his development process. Here's everything he's published so far, all in the last three weeks: 2026-11-04 — Twenty years of mod_wsgi, and what comes next 2026-11-05 — A first look at Muru 2026-11-07 — Muru: looking inside the workers 2026-11-08 — Muru: how it fits together 2026-11-09 — Muru: import once, fork many 2026-11-10 — Muru: HTTPS in development 2026-11-11 — Muru: WSGI and ASGI together 2026-11-11 — AI as a lifestyle choice 2026-11-12 — Muru: releases, not restarts 2026-11-13 — Muru: canaries without a service mesh 2026-11-14 — Muru: a better tenant in a container 2026-11-15 — Muru: working with Kubernetes, not around it 2026-11-16 — Muru: scaling from what the workers report 2026-11-17 — Muru: scaling to zero 2026-11-18 — Muru: overlays on a schedule 2026-11-19 — Muru: noticing and responding 2026-11-20 — Muru: a toolbar on every page 2026-11-21 — Muru: tracing in the toolbar 2026-11-22 — Muru: when lazy imports help That post about AI as a lifestyle choice is particularly worth a read: The AI may be doing a lot of the work on the surface, but deciding what isn't good enough yet is still down to me, and twenty years of getting things wrong with mod_wsgi turns out to be useful for that. I am prepared to put in the hard work to keep polishing Muru until it is something I would trust, and something you would too. Tags: graham-dum

Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater. [...] Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line. items.title: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)
items.summary: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube) Claire Vo runs ChatPRD , an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time. In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post ) Claire describes the flood of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent. I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps. Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter. Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse. Tags: youtube , ai , generative-ai , llms , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , ai-misuse

items.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released
items.summary: PostgreSQL 19 Released Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse. This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one: For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary. In practice, that looks like this: UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama'; SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn(); That returns a value like 0/0306EE20 . Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do: WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s'); SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama'; The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time. I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia , which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication: In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it. items.title: llm-gemini 0.38
items.summary: Release: llm-gemini 0.38 Today Google introduced Gemini 4 Neon . I wrote recently about how confusing the pricing for the Gemini 4 series was - Neon has somehow made this even worse. Previously the Gemini 4 lineup was Hydrogen, Argon, and Carbon - where Argon and Carbon were the same price , and Hydrogen was 3/4 of that price now but will be 1/4 of that price when the other two double an 1st December once their initial discount pricing expires. The Neon announcement pretends that Argon doesn't exist. Here's their new image explaining the model line-up: So the lineup now, from most to least expensive, is Carbon, Neon, Hydrogen. Except Carbon is currently half price, so right now Neon ($3/million input, $15/million output) is the most expensive of the three - then Carbon ($2/$10), then Hydrogen ($1.50/$7.50). I guess this will make more sense when Carbon doubles to $4/$20 on December 1st. I ran some pelicans through the three reasoning levels for Neon - low, medium, high. I dropped Argon from my Gemini 4 comparison grid - here's the new Gemini 4 lineup, where the Neon pelicans do look better than Hydrogen and worse than Carbon: As I've done with several recent models , I also fired the following prompt against Gemini 4 Neon on "extra" effort level in Google Antigravity: Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data Here's the result . items.sourceEvidence: Presentiamo GPT‑6.2 Astra e Sol: risultati migliori nel lavoro professionale, capacità di programmazione e di uso del computer più avanzate e maggiore efficienza, a un costo inferiore in ChatGPT Work, Codex e nell’API. Le sue slide, i suoi fogli di calcolo e i suoi documenti sembrano meno generati dall'IA e seguono più fedelmente i modelli che fornisci e le convenzioni del tuo settore. Scrive codice più pulito e crea frontend migliori nell'aspetto e nel funzionamento, soprattutto per siti web, giochi e progettazione 3D. In Agents’ Last Exam, che mette alla prova i modelli su attività professionali articolate in più passaggi, GPT‑6.2 Astra stabilisce un nuovo record, superando GPT‑6 Astra di 5,2 punti a meno di un terzo del costo e Claude Fable 5.2 di 5,5 punti ad appena il 5% del costo. items.title: datasette-arrows 0.1a0
items.summary: Release: datasette-arrows 0.1a0 Datasette 1.0a43 added the ability for plugins to implement streaming export formats. Datasette core supports streaming CSV and TSV - you can export millions of lines of data from a table without needing to load it all into memory, because those two file formats support streaming data in chunks. The register_output_renderer() plugin hook can now be used to implement the same pattern for other formats. I've learned never to release a new plugin feature without accompanying it with a plugin that uses it. Claude Fable 5.2 suggested the Apache Arrow streaming format as a good option, and built this plugin in almost a single shot. Add the plugin to Datasette ( datasette install datasette-arrows ) and the export dialog gains this new Arrow option: This screenshot is from Datasette's main branch - the most recent release doesn't yet group streaming formats such as Arrow with the TSV and CSV in the "All rows in this table" section, but that's coming in the next alpha release. items.summary: External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant , the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects . My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package! Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running: I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches. Tags: sandboxing , security

items.title: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol
items.summary: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol OpenAI: We’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work. They're available in the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol . I shipped LLM 0.38 with support for the new models. 6.2 Astra is 80% of the price of 6 Astra - $8/MTok input and $40/MTok output, the same price as Claude Fable 5.2 (which was also 80% of its predecessor). 6 Astra and Fable 5 were both $10/$50. The cached price is an even bigger discount - $0.40/million compared to $1/million for the older model. This is great news for longer running agentic sessions. items.title: Buying Tokens vs Building an AI Factory with Sadeepa Wijesekara - #785
items.summary: An AI agent can make many model calls to finish a single job. Some need frontier reasoning. Others can run on an open-weight model, and some involve data that has to stay in-house. How do you decide which inference to buy and which to run yourself? Sadeepa Wijesekara, who leads engineering for HPE Private Cloud AI, joins Sam Charrington to discuss how enterprises make those decisions. They get into what it takes to see the cost of individual calls, how teams route work between hosted and local models, and when running your own GPUs makes economic sense. Sadeepa shares how HPE routes coding requests through a single internal endpoint that can send work to a frontier provider or serve it locally. 🗒️ Full show notes: ⁠⁠⁠https://twimlai.com/go/785.
items.podcastDescription: Ricerca, machine learning e applicazioni raccontati da ricercatori e professionisti.

it.title: Comprare token o costruire una fabbrica di IA?
it.summary: In questo episodio, Sadeepa Wijesekara di HPE Private Cloud AI discute con Sam Charrington le strategie aziendali per decidere se acquistare servizi di inferenza o gestire modelli in proprio. L'analisi esplora i costi delle chiamate ai modelli e il routing del lavoro tra sistemi locali e cloud.
it.why_it_matters: Le aziende affrontano scelte complesse per bilanciare la privacy dei dati, le esigenze di ragionamento avanzato e la sostenibilità economica dei carichi di lavoro di intelligenza artificiale.
it.extended_analysis:
I moderni agenti di intelligenza artificiale richiedono una gestione articolata delle chiamate ai modelli, alternando modelli di frontiera e opzioni open-weight in base alla complessità del compito e alla riservatezza dei dati.

Sadeepa Wijesekara condivide l'esperienza di HPE nella gestione di endpoint interni per il routing delle richieste di codifica, offrendo spunti pratici su quando l'investimento in GPU locali diventi economicamente vantaggioso rispetto all'acquisto di token esterni.

Il panorama descritto evidenzia la necessità per i team di ingegneria di monitorare con precisione i costi operativi e di implementare un'infrastruttura flessibile capace di adattarsi a esigenze computazionali eterogenee.
it.context: Il dibattito riflette la crescente maturità dell'adozione aziendale dell'IA, in cui l'efficienza dei costi e la sovranità dei dati guidano le decisioni infrastrutturali dei reparti tecnologici.
key_takeaways: Criteri per scegliere tra modelli ospitati e locali.
Analisi dei costi associati alle chiamate individuali dei modelli.
Strategie di routing per richieste di codifica tramite endpoint interni.
highlights: Sadeepa Wijesekara guida l'ingegneria per HPE Private Cloud AI.
Discussione condotta da Sam Charrington all'interno del podcast TWIML AI.

en.title: Buying Tokens vs Building an AI Factory
en.summary: Sadeepa Wijesekara of HPE Private Cloud AI joins Sam Charrington to explore how enterprises decide between purchasing inference tokens or operating their own AI infrastructure. The discussion covers cost tracking for model calls, workload routing, and the economics of running local GPUs.
en.why_it_matters: Organizations must carefully balance data privacy, advanced reasoning requirements, and economic viability when scaling artificial intelligence operations.
en.extended_analysis:
Modern AI agents execute numerous model calls per task, forcing engineering teams to choose between frontier reasoning capabilities and open-weight models based on data sensitivity and performance needs.

Sadeepa Wijesekara details how HPE routes coding requests through internal endpoints capable of dispatching work to external providers or local servers, illustrating practical enterprise architecture choices.

The conversation sheds light on the granular cost tracking required to optimize AI operations and determine when owning dedicated hardware makes strategic sense.
en.context: This episode addresses the architectural and financial challenges enterprises face as they move from experimental AI deployments to scaled production environments.
key_takeaways: Frameworks for deciding between hosted inference and local execution.
Methods for tracking the cost of individual model calls.
Internal routing strategies for enterprise coding tasks.
highlights: Featuring Sadeepa Wijesekara, engineering lead for HPE Private Cloud AI.
Hosted by Sam Charrington on The TWIML AI Podcast.

es.title: ¿Comprar tokens o construir una fábrica de IA?
es.summary: Sadeepa Wijesekara, de HPE Private Cloud AI, se une a Sam Charrington para analizar cómo las empresas deciden entre comprar inferencia o gestionar su propia infraestructura. La charla aborda el coste de las llamadas a los modelos y el enrutamiento de cargas de trabajo.
es.why_it_matters: Las organizaciones se enfrentan a decisiones críticas para equilibrar la privacidad de los datos, las necesidades de razonamiento avanzado y la rentabilidad económica al escalar la inteligencia artificial.
es.extended_analysis:
Los agentes de IA actuales realizan múltiples llamadas a modelos para completar tareas, lo que exige a los equipos de ingeniería decidir cuándo utilizar modelos open-weight o de frontera según la confidencialidad de los datos.

Sadeepa Wijesekara comparte cómo HPE enruta las solicitudes de código a través de un punto de enlace interno que puede derivar el trabajo a proveedores externos o servidores locales, mostrando enfoques prácticos de arquitectura.

La conversación destaca la importancia de monitorizar los costes individuales y evaluar cuándo resulta económicamente viable la inversión en GPU propias.
es.context: El episodio refleja los desafíos económicos y técnicos a los que se enfrentan las empresas en su transición hacia despliegues de IA más maduros y controlados.
key_takeaways: Criterios para elegir entre modelos alojados y locales.
Seguimiento de costes en llamadas individuales de modelos.
Estrategias de enrutamiento para tareas de programación.
highlights: Sadeepa Wijesekara lidera la ingeniería en HPE Private Cloud AI.
Conversación conducida por Sam Charrington en The TWIML AI Podcast.

de.title: Token kaufen oder eine KI-Fabrik bauen?
de.summary: Sadeepa Wijesekara von HPE Private Cloud AI diskutiert mit Sam Charrington, wie Unternehmen zwischen dem Kauf von Inferenzdiensten und dem Betrieb eigener Modelle abwägen. Im Fokus stehen Kostenanalysen für Modellaufrufe und Workload-Routing.
de.why_it_matters: Unternehmen müssen bei der Skalierung von Künstlicher Intelligenz Datenschutz, Anforderungen an fortgeschrittenes Reasoning und wirtschaftliche Rentabilität sorgfältig ausbalancieren.
de.extended_analysis:
Moderne KI-Agenten führen oft zahlreiche Modellaufrufe aus, um eine Aufgabe zu bewältigen. Entwicklungsteams müssen daher entscheiden, wann sie auf Frontier-Modelle oder Open-Weight-Alternativen zurückgreifen.

Sadeepa Wijesekara erläutert, wie HPE Kodierungsanfragen über einen internen Endpunkt leitet, der Arbeiten an externe Anbieter übergeben oder lokal ausführen kann, was praktische Einblicke in die Unternehmensarchitektur bietet.

Das Gespräch verdeutlicht, wie wichtig die genaue Überwachung einzelner Aufrufkosten ist, um fundierte Entscheidungen über eigene GPU-Investitionen zu treffen.
de.context: Die Episode beleuchtet die architektonischen und finanziellen Abwägungen, mit denen Unternehmen beim Übergang zu produktionsreifen KI-Systemen konfrontiert sind.
key_takeaways: Entscheidungskriterien zwischen gehosteter Inferenz und lokalem Betrieb.
Methoden zur Verfolgung der Kosten einzelner Modellaufrufe.
Interne Routing-Strategien für Programmieraufgaben.

it.title: Costruire l'intelligenza visiva con Black Forest Labs
it.summary: Cosa può imparare un modello sul mondo osservando video e ascoltando audio? Andreas Blattmann e Dustin Podell di Black Forest Labs parlano con swyx dell'addestramento di FLUX 3 su immagini, video e audio combinati.
it.why_it_matters: Questo episodio esplora come l'addestramento multimodale con video e audio apra nuove prospettive nella comprensione visiva e nella percezione del mondo da parte dei modelli.
it.extended_analysis:
Nel podcast Latent Space, gli ospiti Andreas Blattmann e Dustin Podell di Black Forest Labs discutono con il conduttore swyx del loro approccio innovativo allo sviluppo di FLUX 3. Al centro della conversazione c'è l'idea che l'intelligenza visiva possa essere ampliata integrando dati multimediali eterogenei.

La discussione evidenzia come l'analisi combinata di immagini, sequenze video e tracce audio consenta ai modelli di catturare dinamiche complesse del mondo reale, come il movimento della telecamera che rivela dettagli nascosti.
it.context: Il panorama dell'intelligenza artificiale generativa si sta evolvendo rapidamente verso sistemi sempre più multimodali, in grado di elaborare simultaneamente input visivi e sonori.
key_takeaways: Black Forest Labs ha addestrato FLUX 3 utilizzando immagini, video e audio insieme.
L'addestramento multimodale esplora cosa un modello può apprendere osservando e ascoltando il mondo.
Un movimento di telecamera in un video può rivelare lati nascosti o prospettive non visibili nelle immagini statiche.
highlights: Ospiti dell'episodio: Andreas Blattmann e Dustin Podell.
Condotto da swyx per il podcast Latent Space.

en.title: Building Visual Intelligence with Black Forest Labs
en.summary: What can a model learn about the world by watching video and listening to audio? Andreas Blattmann and Dustin Podell join swyx to discuss training FLUX 3 on images, video, and audio together.
en.why_it_matters: This episode sheds light on how combining multiple data modalities like video and audio helps models develop a deeper, more dynamic understanding of the physical world.
en.extended_analysis:
In this episode of Latent Space, guests Andreas Blattmann and Dustin Podell from Black Forest Labs sit down with host swyx to explain the methodology behind FLUX 3. They discuss the unique insights gained when a model is trained simultaneously on images, video, and audio streams.

The conversation emphasizes how incorporating moving visuals and sound allows models to perceive dimensions and actions—such as a moving camera revealing hidden perspectives—that static imagery alone cannot capture.
en.context: The AI research community is increasingly moving beyond unimodal models, aiming for richer integration of visual and auditory data to improve world modeling.
key_takeaways: Black Forest Labs trained FLUX 3 on a combination of images, video, and audio.
Multimodal training helps models learn complex spatial and physical dynamics.
Video inputs, such as moving cameras, provide spatial context beyond static images.
highlights: Featuring guests Andreas Blattmann and Dustin Podell.
Hosted by swyx on Latent Space.

es.title: Construyendo inteligencia visual con Black Forest Labs
